1	\section{Discussion}
2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	\label{sec:why_kstar}
4	\label{sec:one_wash}
5	\label{sec:negative_graduated}
6	\label{sec:repr_dependence}
7	\label{sec:boundary_cases}
8	\label{sec:length_confound}
9	
10	\begin{figure}[t]
11	\centering
12	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_jsd_decay.pdf}
13	\caption{Token-level JSD between adjacent depth pairs on log scale. Blue band: min-max range across 8 C4 models (1B--14B) with $\Kempirical{=}2$; dashed purple: Mistral-7B ($\Kempirical{=}1$, cross-scorer validated); green: arXiv Pythia ($\Kempirical{=}3$); dotted red: retrain-chain ($\Kempirical{\geq}4$). C4 models exhibit a sharp cliff ($\lambda \approx 2.2$--$3.5$), while arXiv decays gradually ($\lambda \approx 1.0$) and retrain-chain shows no cliff ($\lambda = 0.285$).}
14	\label{fig:jsd_decay}
15	\end{figure}
16	
17	\paragraph{One-wash laundering (web text).}
18	For general web text, $\Kempirical{=}2$ reflects concentrated information loss: 0v1 is near-trivially separable ($\auc \geq 0.92$), 1v2 drops by ${\sim}$30\,pp, and 2v3 falls below $\theta$.
19	A single generation pass renders text indistinguishable from multiply recycled content, limiting depth-aware curation to a binary boundary.
20	Converging evidence supports a data-intrinsic interpretation: OBD achieves 96\% depth-0 recall but only 14--22\% for depths 2--4; frontier LLMs show 8--38\% (McNemar $p > 0.05$ vs.\ OBD; Table~\ref{tab:s3_llm_zeroshot}).
21	Replacing OBD-LightGBM with logistic regression, linear SVC, or random forest yields non-significant differences in 31/36 model $\times$ classifier comparisons (Table~\ref{tab:mcnemar_obd_baselines}); depth discriminability is feature-driven.
22	
23	\paragraph{JSD decay and the discrimination boundary.}
24	Token-level Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) between adjacent generations reveals two distinct decay regimes (Figure~\ref{fig:jsd_decay}): C4 models exhibit a sharp cliff (0v1 JSD exceeds 1v2 by 6--56$\times$, median ${\sim}$15$\times$) followed by rapid convergence to a noise floor, while arXiv decays ${\sim}$3$\times$ slower ($\lambda \approx 1.0$ vs.\ $2.9$).
25	Cross-model consistency indicates that $G_\delta$ contraction rate is domain-governed.
26	The retrain-chain profile ($\lambda = 0.285$, no cliff) reflects model-adaptation artifacts rather than text-intrinsic loss: retrain-chain $\Kempirical{\geq}4$ (Pythia-1.4B LoRA; Table~\ref{tab:retrain_ci}) far exceeds prompt-chain $\Kempirical{=}2$ (Appendix~\ref{sec:jsd_extended}).
27	
28	\paragraph{Prompt-chain as a conservative bound.}
29	All main results use prompt-chain generation, which isolates text-intrinsic degradation from training dynamics.
30	Retrain-chain validation (Pythia-1.4B LoRA) yields $\Kempirical{\geq}4$ (Table~\ref{tab:retrain_ci}), substantially exceeding prompt-chain $\Kempirical{=}2$, because cumulative model-adaptation artifacts provide additional depth signal absent from prompt-chain.
31	Real-world contamination involves both mechanisms; prompt-chain $\Kempirical$ is therefore a conservative lower bound on field-observable discriminability.
32	
33	\paragraph{Graduated filtering failure.}
34	For web text, 2v3 $\auc < \theta$ across all model configurations, so depth assignments for $d \geq 2$ approximate random labels; graduated weighting injects noise; this explains the convergence toward binary at high $\alpha$ (Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_limitations}).
35	The strategy ordering binary $>$ graduated aligns with the $\Kempirical{=}2$ prediction: graduated approaches cannot exploit depth information that does not exist beyond the discrimination boundary.
36	On arXiv ($\Kempirical{=}3$), graduated filtering similarly shows no improvement over unfiltered data, consistent with $\Kempirical$ capturing discriminability rather than curation utility.
37	DSIR fails differently: bigram hashing captures domain shift but not depth-correlated signatures (pattern persists across 10--50\% contamination ratios; Appendix~\ref{sec:dose_response}).
38	
39	\paragraph{Representation and scorer dependence.}
40	$\Kempirical$ is representation-dependent: frozen Qwen embeddings yield $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$, while Pythia and OLMo match the 15D boundary at $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 2$ (Table~\ref{tab:neural_probe_crossmodel}); the 15D features trade one depth level for cross-model consistency (8/9 configurations $\Kempirical{\leq}2$).
41	$\Kempirical$ can also depend on scorer family: on Wikipedia, cross-family scoring reduces $\Kempirical$ from 2 to 1 ($\Delta = -2.4$\,pp; Appendix~\ref{sec:wiki_domain}), while on C4 it preserves feature rankings ($\rho > 0.90$) and $\Kempirical$ for 6/8 configurations (Section~\ref{sec:transfer}).
42	Scorer sensitivity is inversely related to domain lexical diversity; we recommend cross-family validation for new domains.
43	
44	\paragraph{Domain dependence of $\Kempirical$.}
45	C4 web text yields $\Kempirical{=}2$ (8/9 configurations, 1B--14B), while arXiv yields $\Kempirical{=}3$ across five models and four architecture families (Section~\ref{sec:cross_domain}).
46	With scorer confound controlled, all six models yield $\Kempirical{=}1$ on Wikipedia (Appendix~\ref{sec:wiki_domain}), producing a consistent ordering by source domain: arXiv ($\Kempirical{=}3$) $>$ C4 ($\Kempirical{=}2$) $>$ Wikipedia ($\Kempirical{=}1$), which correlates with domain-level lexical diversity (Table~\ref{tab:domain-ttr-entropy}).
47	The only C4 exception (Mistral-7B, $\Kempirical{=}1$) has $\Kempirical{=}3$ on arXiv, reinforcing the domain-governed interpretation (Appendix~\ref{sec:boundary_extended}).
48	A LaTeX markup ablation confirms that content-level properties dominate (2v3 $\Delta = -1.8$\,pp, $\Kempirical$ unchanged; Appendix~\ref{sec:latex_ablation}).
49	
50	
51	\paragraph{Why $\Kempirical$ matters.}
52	$\Kempirical{=}2$ for web text is not a negative result but a precise measurement: it rules out both $\Kempirical{=}1$ (no depth signal beyond 0v1) and $\Kempirical{\geq}3$ (graduated tracking feasible), while arXiv $\Kempirical{=}3$ confirms the framework captures real domain-level variation rather than a methodological ceiling.
53	$\Kempirical$ thus serves as an empirical diagnostic of domain properties and is directly prescriptive for curation granularity.
54	The method combines established components (LightGBM, hand-crafted features, ordinal decomposition); the contribution is the measurement framework and the empirical characterization it enables.
55	
56	
57	
58	\paragraph{Practical implications.}
59	For web text ($\Kempirical{=}2$), graduated depth weighting injects noise beyond the boundary, validating binary filtering as optimal (Section~\ref{sec:filtering}); for arXiv ($\Kempirical{=}3$), an additional depth level carries discriminative signal.
60	Mixed-domain corpora thus require domain-stratified filtering; $\Kempirical{=}2$ provides post-hoc grounding for the binary approach of \citet{drayson2025}.
61

frontier LLMs show 8--38\\% (McNemar $p > 0.05$ vs.\\ OBD; Table~\\ref{tab:s3_llm_zeroshot}).\nBaseline classifier substitution (logistic regression, linear SVC, random forest) yields non-significant McNemar differences in 31/36 comparisons (Table~\\ref{tab:mcnemar_obd_baselines}).\n\n\\paragraph{JSD decay and the discrimination boundary.}\nToken-level Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) between adjacent generations reveals two distinct decay regimes (Figure~\\ref{fig:jsd_decay}): C4 models exhibit a sharp cliff (0v1 JSD exceeds 1v2 by 6--56$\\times$, median ${\\sim}$15$\\times$) followed by rapid convergence to a noise floor, while arXiv decays ${\\sim}$3$\\times$ slower ($\\lambda \\approx 1.0$ vs.\\ $2.9$).\nCross-model consistency indicates that $G_\\delta$ contraction rate is domain-governed.\nThe retrain-chain profile ($\\lambda = 0.285$, no cliff) reflects model-adaptation artifacts rather than text-intrinsic loss: retrain-chain $\\Kempirical{\\geq}4$ (Pythia-1.4B LoRA; Table~\\ref{tab:retrain_ci}) far exceeds prompt-chain $\\Kempirical{=}2$; since all main results use prompt-chain, the reported boundaries are conservative lower bounds (Appendix~\\ref{sec:jsd_extended}).\n\n\\paragraph{Graduated filtering failure.}\nFor web text, 2v3 $\\auc < \\theta$ across all model configurations, so depth assignments for $d \\geq 2$ approximate random labels; graduated weighting injects noise; this explains the convergence toward binary at high $\\alpha$ (Appendix~\\ref{sec:extended_limitations}).\nThe strategy ordering binary $>$ graduated aligns with the $\\Kempirical{=}2$ prediction: graduated approaches cannot exploit depth information that does not exist beyond the discrimination boundary.\nOn arXiv ($\\Kempirical{=}3$), graduated filtering similarly shows no improvement over unfiltered data, consistent with $\\Kempirical$ capturing discriminability rather than curation utility.\nDSIR fails differently: bigram hashing captures domain shift but not depth-correlated signatures (pattern persists across 10--50\\% contamination ratios; Appendix~\\ref{sec:dose_response}).\n\n\\paragraph{Representation and scorer dependence.}\n$\\Kempirical$ is representation-dependent: frozen Qwen embeddings yield $\\Kempirical^{\\text{neural}} = 3$, while Pythia and OLMo match the 15D boundary at $\\Kempirical^{\\text{neural}} = 2$ (Table~\\ref{tab:neural_probe_crossmodel}); the 15D features trade one depth level for cross-model consistency (8/9 configurations $\\Kempirical{\\leq}2$).\n$\\Kempirical$ can also depend on scorer family: on Wikipedia, cross-family scoring reduces $\\Kempirical$ from 2 to 1 ($\\Delta = -2.4$\\,pp; Appendix~\\ref{sec:wiki_domain}), while on C4 it preserves feature rankings ($\\rho > 0.90$) and $\\Kempirical$ for 6/8 configurations (Section~\\ref{sec:transfer}).\nScorer sensitivity is inversely related to domain lexical diversity; we recommend cross-family validation for new domains.\n\n\\paragraph{Domain dependence of $\\Kempirical$.}\nC4 web text yields $\\Kempirical{=}2$ (8/9 configurations, 1B--14B), while arXiv yields $\\Kempirical{=}3$ across five models and four architecture families (Section~\\ref{sec:cross_domain}).\nWith scorer confound controlled, all six models yield $\\Kempirical{=}1$ on Wikipedia (Appendix~\\ref{sec:wiki_domain}), producing a consistent ordering by source domain: arXiv ($\\Kempirical{=}3$) $>$ C4 ($\\Kempirical{=}2$) $>$ Wikipedia ($\\Kempirical{=}1$), which correlates with domain-level lexical diversity (Table~\\ref{tab:domain-ttr-entropy}).\nThe only C4 exception (Mistral-7B, $\\Kempirical{=}1$) has $\\Kempirical{=}3$ on arXiv, reinforcing the domain-governed interpretation (Appendix~\\ref{sec:boundary_extended}).\nA LaTeX markup ablation confirms that content-level properties dominate (2v3 $\\Delta = -1.8$\\,pp, $\\Kempirical$ unchanged; Appendix~\\ref{sec:latex_ablation}).\n\n\n\\paragraph{Why $\\Kempirical$ matters.}\n$\\Kempirical{=}2$ for web text is not a negative result but a precise measurement: it rules out both $\\Kempirical{=}1$ (no depth signal beyond 0v1) and $\\Kempirical{\\geq}3$ (graduated tracking feasible), while arXiv $\\Kempirical{=}3$ confirms the framework captures real domain-level variation rather than a methodological ceiling.\n$\\Kempirical$ thus serves as an empirical diagnostic of domain properties and is directly prescriptive for curation granularity.\nThe method combines established components (LightGBM, hand-crafted features, ordinal decomposition); the contribution is the measurement framework and the empirical characterization it enables.\n\n\n\n\\paragraph{Practical implications.}\nFor web text ($\\Kempirical{=}2$), graduated depth weighting injects noise beyond the boundary, validating binary filtering as optimal (Section~\\ref{sec:filtering}); for arXiv ($\\Kempirical{=}3$), an additional depth level carries discriminative signal.\nMixed-domain corpora thus require domain-stratified filtering; $\\Kempirical{=}2$ provides post-hoc grounding for the binary approach of \\citet{drayson2025}.\n",

    "originalFile": "\\section{Discussion}\n\\label{sec:discussion}\n\\label{sec:why_kstar}\n\\label{sec:one_wash}\n\\label{sec:negative_graduated}\n\\label{sec:repr_dependence}\n\\label{sec:boundary_cases}\n\\label{sec:length_confound}\n\n\\begin{figure}[t]\n\\centering\n\\includegraphics[width=\\columnwidth]{figures/fig_jsd_decay.pdf}\n\\caption{Token-level JSD between adjacent depth pairs on log scale. Blue band: min-max range across 8 C4 models (1B--14B) with $\\Kempirical{=}2$; dashed purple: Mistral-7B ($\\Kempirical{=}1$, cross-scorer validated); green: arXiv Pythia ($\\Kempirical{=}3$); dotted red: retrain-chain ($\\Kempirical{\\geq}4$). C4 models exhibit a sharp cliff ($\\lambda \\approx 2.2$--$3.5$), while arXiv decays gradually ($\\lambda \\approx 1.0$) and retrain-chain shows no cliff ($\\lambda = 0.285$).}\n\\label{fig:jsd_decay}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\paragraph{One-wash laundering (web text).}\nFor general web text, $\\Kempirical{=}2$ reflects concentrated information loss: 0v1 is near-trivially separable ($\\auc \\geq 0.92$), 1v2 drops by ${\\sim}$30\\,pp, and 2v3 falls below $\\theta$.\nA single generation pass renders text indistinguishable from multiply recycled content, limiting depth-aware curation to a binary boundary.\nConverging evidence supports a data-intrinsic interpretation: OBD achieves 96\\% depth-0 recall but only 14--22\\% for depths 2--4; frontier LLMs show 8--38\\% (McNemar $p > 0.05$ vs.\\ OBD; Table~\\ref{tab:s3_llm_zeroshot}).\nBaseline classifier substitution (logistic regression, linear SVC, random forest) yields non-significant McNemar differences in 31/36 comparisons (Table~\\ref{tab:mcnemar_obd_baselines}).\n\n\\paragraph{JSD decay and the discrimination boundary.}\nToken-level Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) between adjacent generations reveals two distinct decay regimes (Figure~\\ref{fig:jsd_decay}): C4 models exhibit a sharp cliff (0v1 JSD exceeds 1v2 by 6--56$\\times$, median ${\\sim}$15$\\times$) followed by rapid convergence to a noise floor, while arXiv decays ${\\sim}$3$\\times$ slower ($\\lambda \\approx 1.0$ vs.\\ $2.9$).\nCross-model consistency indicates that $G_\\delta$ contraction rate is domain-governed.\nThe retrain-chain profile ($\\lambda = 0.285$, no cliff) reflects model-adaptation artifacts rather than text-intrinsic loss: retrain-chain $\\Kempirical{\\geq}4$ (Pythia-1.4B LoRA; Table~\\ref{tab:retrain_ci}) far exceeds prompt-chain $\\Kempirical{=}2$; since all main results use prompt-chain, the reported boundaries are conservative lower bounds (Appendix~\\ref{sec:jsd_extended}).\n\n\\paragraph{Graduated filtering failure.}\nFor web text, 2v3 $\\auc < \\theta$ across all model configurations, so depth assignments for $d \\geq 2$ approximate random labels; graduated weighting injects noise; this explains the convergence toward binary at high $\\alpha$ (Appendix~\\ref{sec:extended_limitations}).\nThe strategy ordering binary $>$ graduated aligns with the $\\Kempirical{=}2$ prediction: graduated approaches cannot exploit depth information that does not exist beyond the discrimination boundary.\nOn arXiv ($\\Kempirical{=}3$), graduated filtering similarly shows no improvement over unfiltered data, consistent with $\\Kempirical$ capturing discriminability rather than curation utility.\n\n\\paragraph{Representation and scorer dependence.}\n$\\Kempirical$ is representation-dependent: frozen Qwen embeddings yield $\\Kempirical^{\\text{neural}} = 3$, while Pythia and OLMo match the 15D boundary at $\\Kempirical^{\\text{neural}} = 2$ (Table~\\ref{tab:neural_probe_crossmodel}); the 15D features trade one depth level for cross-model consistency (8/9 configurations $\\Kempirical{\\leq}2$).\n$\\Kempirical$ can also depend on scorer family: on Wikipedia, cross-family scoring reduces $\\Kempirical$ from 2 to 1 ($\\Delta = -2.4$\\,pp; Appendix~\\ref{sec:wiki_domain}), while on C4 it preserves feature rankings ($\\rho > 0.90$) and $\\Kempirical$ for 6/8 configurations (Section~\\ref{sec:transfer}).\nScorer sensitivity is inversely related to domain lexical diversity; we recommend cross-family validation for new domains.\n\n\\paragraph{Domain dependence of $\\Kempirical$.}\nC4 web text yields $\\Kempirical{=}2$ (8/9 configurations, 1B--14B), while arXiv yields $\\Kempirical{=}3$ across five models and four architecture families (Section~\\ref{sec:cross_domain}).\nWith scorer confound controlled, all six models yield $\\Kempirical{=}1$ on Wikipedia (Appendix~\\ref{sec:wiki_domain}), producing a consistent ordering by source domain: arXiv ($\\Kempirical{=}3$) $>$ C4 ($\\Kempirical{=}2$) $>$ Wikipedia ($\\Kempirical{=}1$), which correlates with domain-level lexical diversity (Table~\\ref{tab:domain-ttr-entropy}).\nThe only C4 exception (Mistral-7B, $\\Kempirical{=}1$) has $\\Kempirical{=}3$ on arXiv, reinforcing the domain-governed interpretation (Appendix~\\ref{sec:boundary_extended}).\nA LaTeX markup ablation confirms that content-level properties dominate (2v3 $\\Delta = -1.8$\\,pp, $\\Kempirical$ unchanged; Appendix~\\ref{sec:latex_ablation}).\n\n\\paragraph{Why $\\Kempirical$ matters.}\n$\\Kempirical{=}2$ for web text is not a negative result but a precise measurement: it rules out both $\\Kempirical{=}1$ (no depth signal beyond 0v1) and $\\Kempirical{\\geq}3$ (graduated tracking feasible), while arXiv $\\Kempirical{=}3$ confirms the framework captures real domain-level variation rather than a methodological ceiling.\n$\\Kempirical$ thus serves as an empirical diagnostic of domain properties; the contribution is the measurement framework and its empirical characterization.\n\n\n\nFor curation, $\\Kempirical{=}2$ validates binary filtering for web text (Section~\\ref{sec:filtering}), while arXiv $\\Kempirical{=}3$ implies an additional exploitable depth level;     "originalFile": "\\section{Introduction}\n\\label{sec:introduction}\n\nWeb-scale text corpora are increasingly contaminated by synthetic content that has itself been generated from earlier synthetic content.\nEstimates suggest that a substantial fraction of online text is machine-generated~\\cite{sun2025aigt, spennemann2025quantifying}, and this share continues to rise.\nWhen models train on the outputs of earlier models, the resulting multi-generational synthetic text degrades with each iteration: tail modes vanish, lexical diversity contracts, and surprisal distributions flatten~\\cite{shumailov2024collapse, dohmatob2024model}.\nThis degradation arises in both \\emph{retrain-chains} (iteratively training on model outputs) and \\emph{prompt-chains} (recursively generating from previous outputs without retraining); we study the latter, which isolates generation-level information loss from training dynamics (Appendix~\\ref{sec:extended_limitations}).\nYet the dominant paradigm treats all machine-generated text identically, discarding the generational depth dimension.\n\nThis gap cuts across multiple communities.\nBinary detectors~\\cite{basani2026diveye, zhang2024minkpp} produce no depth estimate (Section~\\ref{sec:binary_confidence}).\nMembership inference~\\cite{zawalski2026codec} addresses a different question, and the model collapse literature~\\cite{shumailov2024collapse, alemohammad2024selfconsuming, schaeffer2025position} provides no per-text tool.\nData selection methods~\\cite{xie2023dsir, tirumala2023d4, drayson2025} likewise ignore recursive depth.\nNo existing method estimates how many rounds of recursive generation a text has undergone.\n\nKnowing whether the discriminable depth is finite, and where it saturates, has direct practical consequences.\nFor data curation, the saturation point determines filtering granularity: if discrimination collapses at depth 2, graduated weighting beyond that boundary injects noise, and binary filtering becomes the principled choice.\nModel collapse theory predicts monotonic quality degradation across generations, but existing analyses are population-level and provide no per-text measure of where degradation saturates.\n$\\Kempirical$ fills this gap by localizing the generation at which adjacent outputs become empirically indistinguishable.\n\nThe Data Processing Inequality implies that information degrades monotonically across generations, motivating a finite discrimination boundary $\\Kstar$.\nWe empirically measure $\\Kempirical$ (the maximum depth at which a classifier reliably distinguishes adjacent generations) using 15 statistical features computed via a fixed reference scorer (Section~\\ref{sec:features}) and an Ordinal Binary Decomposition (OBD) LightGBM classifier.\nWe operationalize $\\Kempirical$ as the deepest $k \\geq 1$ where the pairwise $\\auc_{k-1,k}$ exceeds $\\theta = 0.60$ preserved across six models spanning four architecture families, three scales (1B--14B), and four decoding strategies, with $\\Kempirical$ consistently varying by source domain
